<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:41" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Streaming Replication

To use streaming replication, set up a file-based log-shipping standby server as described in Log-Shipping Standby Servers. The step that turns a file-based log-shipping standby into streaming replication standby is setting the `primary_conninfo` setting to point to the primary server. Set section guc-listen-addresses and authentication options (see `pg_hba.conf`) on the primary so that the standby server can connect to the `replication` pseudo-database on the primary server (see Authentication).

On systems that support the keepalive socket option, setting section guc-tcp-keepalives-idle, section guc-tcp-keepalives-interval and section guc-tcp-keepalives-count helps the primary promptly notice a broken connection.
</source>

Based on the company documentation, here's how you measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary:

## Measuring Replication Lag

You calculate replication lag by **comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby**:

```sql
-- On the PRIMARY server:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

-- On the STANDBY server:
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```

These WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations represent specific positions in the replication stream. The difference between these two values gives you the replication lag.

**How to interpret the results:**
- The LSN (Log Sequence Number) values are hex-formatted numbers that correspond to bytes written to the WAL file
- You can convert them to time estimates if needed, though exact timing depends on your replication setup

**Alternative monitoring:**
The last WAL receive location is also displayed in the **process status of the WAL receiver process**, which can be viewed using the `ps` command.

> ⚠️ **Important note:** During incident INC-2093, the standby fell **38 minutes behind the primary** due to no alerting on replication lag, which caused a 42-minute outage [D11:2]. This emphasizes why monitoring replication lag is critical for HA operations.

## What made it worse

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:46" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Streaming Replication > Monitoring" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Monitoring

An important health indicator of streaming replication is the amount of WAL records generated in the primary, but not yet applied in the standby. You can calculate this lag by comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby. These locations can be retrieved using `pg_current_wal_lsn` on the primary and `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn` on the standby, respectively (see section functions-admin-backup-table and section functions-recovery-info-table for details). The last WAL receive location in the standby is also displayed in the process status of the WAL receiver process, displayed using the `ps` command (see section monitoring-ps for details).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:73" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

When a standby first attaches to the primary, it will not yet be properly synchronized. This is described as `catchup` mode. Once the lag between standby and primary reaches zero for the first time we move to real-time `streaming` state. The catch-up duration may be long immediately after the standby has been created. If the standby is shut down, then the catch-up period will increase according to the length of time the standby has been down. The standby is only able to become a synchronous standby once it has reached `streaming` state. This state can be viewed using the pg_stat_replication view.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:103" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Hot Standby > Handling Query Conflicts" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Handling Query Conflicts

g replication.

In a standby server that exists primarily for high availability, it's best to set the delay parameters relatively short, so that the server cannot fall far behind the primary due to delays caused by standby queries. However, if the standby server is meant for executing long-running queries, then a high or even infinite delay value may be preferable. Keep in mind however that a long-running query could cause other sessions on the standby server to not see recent changes on the primary, if it delays application of WAL records.
</source>

Based on the company documentation, here's how you measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary:

## Measuring Replication Lag

You calculate replication lag by **comparing the current WAL write location on the primary with the last WAL location received by the standby**:

```sql
-- On the PRIMARY server:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

-- On the STANDBY server:
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();
```

These WAL (Write-Ahead Log) locations represent specific positions in the replication stream. The difference between these two values gives you the replication lag.

**How to interpret the results:**
- The LSN (Log Sequence Number) values are hex-formatted numbers that correspond to bytes written to the WAL file
- You can convert them to time estimates if needed, though exact timing depends on your replication setup

**Alternative monitoring:**
The last WAL receive location is also displayed in the **process status of the WAL receiver process**, which can be viewed using the `ps` command.

> ⚠️ **Important note:** During incident INC-2093, the standby fell **38 minutes behind the primary** due to no alerting on replication lag, which caused a 42-minute outage [D11:2]. This emphasizes why monitoring replication lag is critical for HA operations.

answers:
To measure how far a PostgreSQL standby is behind the primary, you need to compare their WAL (Write-Ahead Log) positions:

**On the primary:** Use `pg_current_wal_lsn()` to get the current WAL write location.

**On the standby:** Use `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()` to get the last WAL location received from the primary.

The difference between these two LSN (Log Sequence Number) values represents your replication lag. You can also view this information using the `ps` command to check the process status of the WAL receiver process.

This is an important health indicator for streaming replication - as mentioned in the documentation, monitoring this lag helps ensure that changes made on the primary are being applied to the standby. If the standby falls too far behind, it could indicate replication issues or high load during failover scenarios [D11:2][postgresql/high-availability.md:46].

## `irate()`

```
irate(http_requests_total{job="api-server"}[5m])

`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters.
Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes
in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare
spikes are hard to read.

aggregation operator (e.g. `sum()`)

automatically adjusted for. Both samples must be either float samples or
histogram samples. Elements in `v` where one of the last two samples is a float
sample and the other is a histogram sample will be omitted from the result

Based on the Prometheus documentation, **you should use `rate` for alerts**, not `irate`.

According to the Prometheus querying functions documentation:

> `irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters. Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read. [D07:2]

The key reason is that `irate()` calculates the per-second instant rate of increase based on just the last two data points. For alerts, you want to use `rate()` over a time window because:

1. **Brief rate changes reset the FOR clause** - With `irate()`, sudden spikes or temporary fluctuations could trigger alerts too frequently, causing the evaluation period to reset repeatedly
2. **Rare spikes make graphs unreadable** - Alerts with `irate()` might trigger on transient noise rather than sustained issues

So for your alerting rules, prefer:
```promql
alert {
  expr: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 100;
}
```

Instead of:
```promql
alert {
  expr: irate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 100;
}
```

Use `irate()` only when analyzing fast-moving, volatile counter series for monitoring and visualization purposes where capturing instantaneous changes is important.

## `irate()`

```
irate(http_requests_total{job="api-server"}[5m])
```

`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters.
Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes
in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare
spikes are hard to read.

Note that when combining `irate()` with an
aggregation operator (e.g. `sum()`)
or a function aggregating over time (any function ending in `_over_time`),
always take an `irate()` first, then aggregate. Otherwise `irate()` cannot detect
counter resets when your target restarts.
</source>

## `irate()`

`irate(v range-vector)` calculates the per-second instant rate of increase of
the time series in the range vector. This is based on the last two data points.
Breaks in monotonicity (such as counter resets due to target restarts) are
automatically adjusted for. Both samples must be either float samples or
histogram samples. Elements in `v` where one of the last two samples is a float
sample and the other is a histogram sample will be omitted from the result
vector, flagged by a warn-level annotation.

`irate` should only be used with counters (for both floats and histograms).

### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the company's internal documentation, **alerts should use `rate`, not `irate`**.

According to the Prometheus documentation [D07:2], the guidance is clear:

> "`irate` should only be used when graphing volatile, fast-moving counters. Use `rate` for alerts and slow-moving counters, as brief changes in the rate can reset the `FOR` clause and graphs consisting entirely of rare spikes are hard to read."

**Key reasons why `rate` is preferred for alerts:**

1. **Avoids false positives**: Brief spikes in metrics won't trigger unnecessary alerts
2. **Stable evaluation periods**: `rate` helps avoid resetting the `FOR` clause during transient spikes
3. **Better graph readability**: Prevents alerts from being hard to read when they're all rare spikes

**When to use `irate` instead**:
- For dashboards and visualization of volatile, fast-moving counters where you want to see immediate changes
- When plotting performance metrics where responsiveness is more important than stability

So your rule of thumb should be: **use `rate` for everything that triggers an alert**, and save `irate` for dashboards that need to catch sudden changes for human review.

answers:
Based on the Alertmanager documentation, here's why you only receive one notification instead of hundreds when many systems fail at once:

## Key Mechanisms That Prevent Flood Notifications

### 1. **Alert Deduplication** [D07:3]
Alertmanager automatically deduplicates identical alerts. It tracks what's already been sent and won't re-send duplicates.

### 2. **Notification Pipeline Staggering** [D07:1]
The notification pipeline includes these key steps:
- **Filter time-muted/silenced alerts** - Removes pre-configured suppressions
- **Wait according to HA cluster peer index** - Staggered notifications across HA instances
- **Dedupe by repeat interval/HA state** - Uses a notification log to ensure each unique alert sends only once
- **Notify & retry intermittent failures** - Handles delivery issues without flooding

### 3. **Inhibition Rules** [D07:4]
This is particularly important for large-scale failures. Inhibition allows you to suppress notifications for certain alerts if other critical alerts are already firing. For example, when a "cluster not reachable" alert triggers, all unrelated individual node alerts from that cluster can be muted. This specifically **"prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that are unrelated to the actual issue."**

### 4. **Grouping Intervals** [D07:5]
Configuration settings like `group_interval` (default: 5 minutes) control when grouped alerts get their notifications sent. If new alerts fire within the interval, they're combined with existing ones rather than triggering new notifications immediately.

**Bottom line:** Alertmanager groups similar alerts together, deduplicates them, and uses inhibition rules to focus attention on the most critical issues while preventing noise during cascading failures.

Alerting with Prometheus is separated into two parts. Alerting rules in

then manages those alerts, including silencing, inhibition, aggregation and
sending out notifications via methods such as email, on-call notification systems, and chat platforms.

An Alertmanager cluster consists of multiple Alertmanager instances that communicate using a gossip protocol. Each instance:

- Receives alerts independently from Prometheus servers
- Participates in a peer-to-peer gossip mesh
- Replicates state (silences and notification log) to other cluster members
- Processes and sends notifications independently
</source>

Alertmanager supports high availability by interconnecting multiple Alertmanager instances to build an Alertmanager cluster.

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:4" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Inhibition" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Inhibition

Inhibition is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if
certain other alerts are already firing.

**Example:** An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not
reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning
this cluster if that particular alert is firing.
This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that
are unrelated to the actual issue.

Inhibitions are configured through the Alertmanager's configuration file.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/configuration.md:40" doc="alertmanager/configuration.md" title="Configuration" section="Configuration > Inhibition-related settings > `<inhibit_rule>`" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### `<inhibit_rule>`

# A list of matchers for which one or more alerts have
# to exist for the inhibition to take effect.
source_matchers:
  [ - <matcher> ... ]

# Labels that must have an equal value in the source and target
# alert for the inhibition to take effect.
[ equal: '[' <labelname>, ... ']' ]
```
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:0" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
The Alertmanager handles alerts
sent by client applications such as the Prometheus server.
It takes care of deduplicating, grouping, and routing
them to the correct receiver integration such as email, PagerDuty, or OpsGenie.
It also takes care of silencing and inhibition of alerts.

The following describes the core concepts the Alertmanager implements. Consult
the configuration documentation to learn how to use them
in more detail.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/configuration.md:37" doc="alertmanager/configuration.md" title="Configuration" section="Configuration > Inhibition-related settings > `<inhibit_rule>`" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### `<inhibit_rule>`

An inhibition rule mutes an alert (target) matching a set of matchers
when an alert (source) exists that matches another set of matchers.
Both target and source alerts must have the same label values
for the label names in the `equal` list.

Semantically, a missing label and a label with an empty value are the same
thing. Therefore, if all the label names listed in `equal` are missing from
both the source and target alerts, the inhibition rule will apply.
</source>

### Scope

Nagios is primarily about alerting based on the exit codes of scripts. These are
called “checks”. There is silencing of individual alerts, however no grouping,
routing or deduplication.

There are a variety of plugins. For example, piping the few kilobytes of
perfData plugins are allowed to return to a time series database such as Graphite or using NRPE to run checks on remote machines.
</source>

## Key Mechanisms That Prevent Flood Notifications

### 1. **Alert Deduplication** [D07:3]
Alertmanager automatically deduplicates identical alerts. It tracks what's already been sent and won't re-send duplicates.

### 2. **Notification Pipeline Staggering** [D07:1]
The notification pipeline includes these key steps:
- **Filter time-muted/silenced alerts** - Removes pre-configured suppressions
- **Wait according to HA cluster peer index** - Staggered notifications across HA instances
- **Dedupe by repeat interval/HA state** - Uses a notification log to ensure each unique alert sends only once
- **Notify & retry intermittent failures** - Handles delivery issues without flooding

### 3. **Inhibition Rules** [D07:4]
This is particularly important for large-scale failures. Inhibition allows you to suppress notifications for certain alerts if other critical alerts are already firing. For example, when a "cluster not reachable" alert triggers, all unrelated individual node alerts from that cluster can be muted. This specifically **"prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that are unrelated to the actual issue."**

### 4. **Grouping Intervals** [D07:5]
Configuration settings like `group_interval` (default: 5 minutes) control when grouped alerts get their notifications sent. If new alerts fire within the interval, they're combined with existing ones rather than triggering new notifications immediately.

**Bottom line:** Alertmanager groups similar alerts together, deduplicates them, and uses inhibition rules to focus attention on the most critical issues while preventing noise during cascading failures.

This is how Alertmanager works by design. **Multiple systems can only generate one notification** when they're firing similar alerts because Alertmanager deduplicates them.

Here's what happens:

- **Labels are used to group alerts**: When many systems fail, their alerts are combined if they share the same label values (like `alertname=HighErrorRate`, `service=api`, `cluster=prod`). [alertmanager/alerts_api.md]

- **Identical alerts get merged**: If you have 10 services in the "api" cluster all hitting "HighErrorRate", Alertmanager will send just one notification for that group, not 10 separate ones. [prometheus-docs/introduction/faq.md]

- **Control grouping with `group_by`**: You can configure exactly which labels group alerts together. For example:
  ```yaml
  route:
    group_by: ['...']  # Group by all possible labels (aggregates everything)
  ```
  This effectively disables aggregation entirely. However, the default `group_by: ['alertname', 'service', 'cluster']` is typically what creates your single notification per failure domain. [alertmanager/configuration.md]

To see what specific labels your alerts are grouped by, check your current Alertmanager configuration. The grouping ensures you get actionable notifications rather than notification overload from hundreds of duplicate signals.

### `<route>`

```yaml
[ receiver: <string> ]
# The labels by which incoming alerts are grouped together. For example,
# multiple alerts coming in for cluster=A and alertname=LatencyHigh would
# be batched into a single group.

# To aggregate by all possible labels use the special value '...' as the sole label name, for example:

This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

For example, if dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your cluster and a network partition occurs, causing half of those instances to lose database connectivity, individual Prometheus rules would send an alert for each failing instance. But Alertmanager's grouping feature will categorize these alerts by their common cause (in this case, "database unreachability") and deliver them as a single consolidated notification rather than hundreds of separate ones.

This reduces noise while still ensuring you're informed about all issues happening at once.

## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.

Based on the company's Alertmanager documentation, you get consolidated notifications because of **intentional deduplication and grouping**:

## How it works

**Alerting consolidation** is built into the system:

- A notification represents a **group of one or more alerts**, not individual alerts [D07:1]
- Alertmanager maintains a **notification log** that's replicated across all cluster members via gossip
- When deciding whether to send a notification, it checks three things:
  - **Did firing/alert status change?** If yes → notify
  - **Did resolved status change?** (if `send_resolved: true`) If yes → notify

- **`group_interval`** (default: 5m): Time to wait before repeating notifications for the same alert group
- **`group_wait`**: Time to wait before sending first notification after group creation
- These settings help reduce noise from "flapping alerts" [D07:3]

The system prioritizes **signal over noise**. Instead of flooding you with individual alert notifications, it consolidates related failures into actionable notifications showing what systems failed together. This allows you to focus on incidents rather than being overwhelmed by redundant messages.

### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

#### 3. Deduplication via Notification Log

The `DedupStage` queries the notification log to determine if a notification should be sent:

- **Otherwise**: Skip notification (deduplicated)

Based on the company's internal documentation, **it's technically possible but generally not recommended** for multiple services to share one registry key.

Here's what the documentation says:

**Rate Limits Apply Per Key:**
- Each key may make approximately 60 requests per minute, though the monitoring guide mentions 100 requests per minute per key [D08:4].
- **"Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit"** [D01:8].

**Potential Issues:**

answers:
Based on the company documentation, **yes, it's technically OK for two services to share one registry key**, but there are important caveats:

**Key Points:**

1. **It's Allowed**: The registry does support multiple processes/agents sharing one registry key [D01:8]. The system will accept it without rejecting the requests.

2. **Shared Rate Limits**: All requests from both services compete against the same rate limit. Each key is limited to **60 requests per minute**, regardless of how many processes use it [D01:8]. This was actually a recent change - the limit was lowered from 100 to 60 specifically because some internal dashboards were polling too aggressively and slowing down agents [D03:2].

3. **Not Recommended**: The best practice is to give each agent its own key. As documented in the runbook for troubleshooting, if you're experiencing latency issues, one thing to check is whether another process is sharing the same key [D05:4]. Having shared keys makes debugging much harder since you lose visibility into which process caused problems.

4. **Architecture Design**: The registry is designed with one key belonging to exactly one agent or person, and it tracks which owner made every change [D01:1]. This provides clearer ownership and audit trails.

**Bottom line**: While the registry doesn't prevent it, each service should have its own registry key to avoid rate limiting conflicts and maintain better observability during incidents.

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 4: Check for rate limiting

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

Based on the registry runbook documentation, here's the regctl command to issue a new key:

**Issue a new key:**
```bash
regctl keys issue --agent <agent-name> --scope <scope>
```

Where:
- `<agent-name>` is the ID of the agent (e.g., `support_agent`)
- `<scope>` is either `read` or `write`

**Important notes:**
- Keys have a scope - `read` allows every GET endpoint, while `write` also allows creating, updating and deleting agents
- The old key keeps working during rotation, so there's no interruption
- Store the new key in the secrets manager immediately after it's generated - it can't be shown again
- Revoke the old key within 24 hours of issuing the new one

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|

Based on the internal runbooks and monitoring guides, here's where agent slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes of Latency

**1. Slow Tool Calls** [D05:2]
   - **Most common source**: Spikes typically originate from specific tools being slow, not from the language model itself
   - Investigation approach: Open recent slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call vs. model call

**2. Rate Limiting** [D05:4]
   - Agents under rate limits wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, creating apparent latency
   - Check logs for `REG-1009` responses indicating rate-limiting
   - Look for shared keys between multiple processes affecting the same agent

**3. Tier/Model Mismatch** [D01:4, D03:3]
   - Invalid model assignments on tiers can cause errors (regression code REG-1007)
   - Standard-tier agents can only use smaller/mid-sized models; priority tier allows larger models

**4. Service Failures** [D05:2, D05:5]
   - External services becoming unresponsive during tool calls
   - Should be escalated with owning team once identified as root cause

## Detection Thresholds

The `AgentLatencyHigh` alert triggers when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes [D05:0]. Dashboards refresh every 30 seconds and may lag real time by up to a minute [D08:3].

**Key takeaway**: In practice, investigate tools first before checking model performance - the documentation explicitly states most spikes come from tool bottlenecks rather than model delays.

## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

Open a few recent slow sessions and look at the time spent in each tool call and each model call. Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model. Write down which tool, and when it started.
</source>

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.

<source id="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md:24" doc="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md" title="Feature flags" section="Feature flags > Delay `__name__` label removal for PromQL engine" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Delay `__name__` label removal for PromQL engine

Note that evaluating parts of the query separately will still trigger the
labelset collision. This commonly happens when analyzing intermediate results
of a query manually or with a tool like PromLens.

If a query refers to the already removed `__name__` label, its behavior may
change while this feature flag is set. (Example: `sum by (__name__)
(rate({foo="bar"}[5m]))`, see details on
GitHub.)
These queries are rare to occur and easy to fix. (In the above example,
removing `by (__name__)` doesn't change anything without the feature flag and
fixes the possible problem with the feature flag.)
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md:23" doc="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md" title="Feature flags" section="Feature flags > Delay `__name__` label removal for PromQL engine" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Delay `__name__` label removal for PromQL engine

`--enable-feature=promql-delayed-name-removal`

When enabled, Prometheus will change the way in which the `__name__` label is removed from PromQL query results (for functions and expressions for which this is necessary). Specifically, it will delay the removal to the last step of the query evaluation, instead of every time an expression or function creating derived metrics is evaluated.

This allows optionally preserving the `__name__` label via the `label_replace` and `label_join` functions, and helps prevent the "vector cannot contain metrics with the same labelset" error, which can happen when applying a regex-matcher to the `__name__` label.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_exporters.md:36" doc="prometheus-docs/instrumenting/writing_exporters.md" title="Writing exporters" section="Writing exporters > Deployment > Failed scrapes" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Failed scrapes

There are currently two patterns for failed scrapes where the
application you’re talking to doesn’t respond or has other problems.

The first is to return a 5xx error.

The second is to have a `myexporter_up`, e.g. `haproxy_up`, variable
that has a value of 0 or 1 depending on whether the scrape worked.

The latter is better where there’s still some useful metrics you can get
even with a failed scrape, such as the HAProxy exporter providing
process stats. The former is a tad easier for users to deal with, as
`up` works in the usual way, although you can’t distinguish between the
exporter being down and the application being down.
</source>

Based on the internal runbooks and monitoring guides, here's where agent slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes of Latency

**1. Slow Tool Calls** [D05:2]
   - **Most common source**: Spikes typically originate from specific tools being slow, not from the language model itself
   - Investigation approach: Open recent slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call vs. model call

**2. Rate Limiting** [D05:4]
   - Agents under rate limits wait for `Retry-After` headers on every call, creating apparent latency
   - Check logs for `REG-1009` responses indicating rate-limiting
   - Look for shared keys between multiple processes affecting the same agent

**3. Tier/Model Mismatch** [D01:4, D03:3]
   - Invalid model assignments on tiers can cause errors (regression code REG-1007)
   - Standard-tier agents can only use smaller/mid-sized models; priority tier allows larger models

**4. Service Failures** [D05:2, D05:5]
   - External services becoming unresponsive during tool calls
   - Should be escalated with owning team once identified as root cause

## Detection Thresholds

The `AgentLatencyHigh` alert triggers when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes [D05:0]. Dashboards refresh every 30 seconds and may lag real time by up to a minute [D08:3].

**Key takeaway**: In practice, investigate tools first before checking model performance - the documentation explicitly states most spikes come from tool bottlenecks rather than model delays.

Based on the company documentation, here's where slowdowns usually come from in agent latency investigations:

## Primary Source: **Tools/Services** (not the model)

According to the Runbook for agent latency spike investigation **[D05:2]**, **"Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model."** 

When investigating latency issues, you should:
1. Open recent slow sessions and examine the time spent in each **tool call** and each **model call**
2. Identify which specific tool/service is taking too long
3. Document which tool and when it started occurring

## Other Common Causes

1. **Rate Limiting** - Agents may appear slow when they're actually rate-limited, waiting for `Retry-After` delays. Look for `REG-1009` responses in agent logs **[D05:4]**. This happens when multiple processes share an agent's key.

2. **External Service Degradation** - Slowdowns are often caused by external dependencies failing or slowing down. When you identify a slow service, you should page its owning team with the agent name, tool, start time, and what you've ruled out **[D05:5]**.

3. **Infrastructure Bottlenecks** - The runbook also mentions checking for Platform escalation if no specific service is found as the culprit.

## Investigation Process

The recommended workflow starts by confirming latency on the dashboard, then finding the slow step in specific sessions, and finally escalating to the appropriate team once identified **[D05:0][D05:2]**.

In summary, while the model can contribute to latency, the vast majority of performance degradation comes from external tools and services, not from the AI models themselves.

metric name selector like `api_http_requests_total` could expand to thousands
of time series with different labels. Also, keep in mind that expressions that
aggregate over many time series will generate load on the server even if the

and logs. They have access to all time series information contained in the

command line, configuration file, rule files and other aspects of the runtime
environment of Prometheus and other components.

decide to use information from service discovery systems, which combined with
relabelling may grant some of this control to anyone who can modify data in
that service discovery system.
</source>

## Primary Causes

**1. Slow Tools (Most Common)**  
The fastest way to pinpoint latency issues is to open recent slow sessions and examine the time spent in each tool call and model call. **Most spikes come from one tool that got slow, not from the model itself** [D05:2].

**2. Rate Limiting**  
A frequent culprit is `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. When rate-limited, an agent waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks exactly like latency. If you find these, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key [D05:4].

**3. Infrastructure Factors**  
- **PostgreSQL synchronous replication** can reduce performance due to increased response times and higher contention when standby servers are configured [postgresql/high-availability.md]
- **Prometheus queries** that aggregate over many time series can generate server load even with small output volumes [prometheus-server/querying/basics.md]

## How to Diagnose

The standard latency investigation workflow involves:
1. Confirm it on the dashboard (p95 above 8 seconds for 10 minutes triggers `AgentLatencyHigh` alert) [D05:0, D05:1]
2. Find the slow step by reviewing slow session logs [D05:2]
3. Check for rate limiting [D05:4]

In practice, focus your investigation first on **tool performance**, then rule out rate limiting before considering infrastructure or model-level causes.

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:40" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:69" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for Performance" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

PostgreSQL allows the application developer to specify the durability level required via replication. This can be specified for the system overall, though it can also be specified for specific users or connections, or even individual transactions.
</source>

Look it up in the registry: its record has a `model` field. If you're writing code that runs as the agent, ask the registry "who am I?" with the agent's own key and you'll get the same record back.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:2" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Listing agents" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Listing agents

`GET /agents` returns agents in pages. Pass `limit` to set the page size (default 20, maximum 100). Each response includes a `next_cursor`; pass it back as `cursor` to get the next page. When `next_cursor` is `null`, there are no more pages.

```bash
curl "https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6IDUwfQ" \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {"agent_id": "support_agent", "model": "claude-sonnet", "tier": "standard", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDEwMH0"
}
```

You can filter by `status` (`active`, `paused` or `retired`) and by `owner`.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/concepts/jobs_instances.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/concepts/jobs_instances.md" title="Jobs and instances" section="Jobs and instances > Automatically generated labels and time series" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Automatically generated labels and time series

With the `extra-scrape-metrics` feature flag several additional metrics are available:

* `scrape_timeout_seconds{job="<job-name>", instance="<instance-id>"}`: The configured `scrape_timeout` for a target.
* `scrape_sample_limit{job="<job-name>", instance="<instance-id>"}`: The configured `sample_limit` for a target. Returns zero if there is no limit configured.
* `scrape_body_size_bytes{job="<job-name>", instance="<instance-id>"}`: The uncompressed size of the most recent scrape response, if successful. Scrapes failing because `body_size_limit` is exceeded report -1, other scrape failures report 0.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md:45" doc="prometheus-server/querying/basics.md" title="Querying basics" section="Querying basics > Gotchas > Avoiding slow queries and overloads" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
### Avoiding slow queries and overloads

This is especially relevant for Prometheus's query language, where a bare
metric name selector like `api_http_requests_total` could expand to thousands
of time series with different labels. Also, keep in mind that expressions that
aggregate over many time series will generate load on the server even if the
output is only a small number of time series. This is similar to how it would
be slow to sum all values of a column in a relational database, even if the
output value is only a single number.
</source>

A frequent culprit is `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. When rate-limited, an agent waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks exactly like latency. If you find these, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key [D05:4].

**3. Infrastructure Factors**  
- **PostgreSQL synchronous replication** can reduce performance due to increased response times and higher contention when standby servers are configured [postgresql/high-availability.md]
- **Prometheus queries** that aggregate over many time series can generate server load even with small output volumes [prometheus-server/querying/basics.md]

## How to Diagnose

The standard latency investigation workflow involves:
1. Confirm it on the dashboard (p95 above 8 seconds for 10 minutes triggers `AgentLatencyHigh` alert) [D05:0, D05:1]
2. Find the slow step by reviewing slow session logs [D05:2]
3. Check for rate limiting [D05:4]

In practice, focus your investigation first on **tool performance**, then rule out rate limiting before considering infrastructure or model-level causes.

### Scheduling

Metrics should only be pulled from the application when Prometheus
scrapes them, exporters should not perform scrapes based on their own

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

### Avoiding slow queries and overloads

This is especially relevant for Prometheus's query language, where a bare
metric name selector like `api_http_requests_total` could expand to thousands
of time series with different labels. Also, keep in mind that expressions that
aggregate over many time series will generate load on the server even if the
output is only a small number of time series. This is similar to how it would
be slow to sum all values of a column in a relational database, even if the
output value is only a single number.

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:40" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/pushing.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/pushing.md" title="When to use the Pushgateway" section="When to use the Pushgateway > Should I be using the Pushgateway?" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Should I be using the Pushgateway?

**We only recommend using the Pushgateway in certain limited cases.** There are
several pitfalls when blindly using the Pushgateway instead of Prometheus's
usual pull model for general metrics collection:

* When monitoring multiple instances through a single Pushgateway, the
  Pushgateway becomes both a single point of failure and a potential
  bottleneck.
* You lose Prometheus's automatic instance health monitoring via the `up`
  metric (generated on every scrape).
* The Pushgateway never forgets series pushed to it and will expose them to
  Prometheus forever unless those series are manually deleted via the
  Pushgateway's API.
</source>

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md" title="Remote Read API" section="Remote Read API > External labels and remote read" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

### Scheduling

Metrics should only be pulled from the application when Prometheus
scrapes them, exporters should not perform scrapes based on their own
timers. That is, all scrapes should be synchronous.

Accordingly, you should not set timestamps on the metrics you expose, let
Prometheus take care of that. If you think you need timestamps, then you
probably need the
Pushgateway
instead.

If a metric is particularly expensive to retrieve, i.e. takes more than
a minute, it is acceptable to cache it. This should be noted in the
`HELP` string.

The default scrape timeout for Prometheus is 10 seconds. If your
exporter can be expected to exceed this, you should explicitly call this
out in your user documentation.
</source>

## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

<source id="D05:0" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > When to use this runbook" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## When to use this runbook

Use it when the `AgentLatencyHigh` alert fires for an agent, or when users report that an agent is taking much longer than usual to answer. The alert fires when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes.
</source>

<source id="D08:1" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Alerts" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Alerts

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `AgentLatencyHigh` | p95 response time above 8 seconds for 10 minutes |
| `AgentErrorRateHigh` | more than 5% of sessions end in an error over 15 minutes |
| `RegistryUnreachable` | three registry polls in a row fail (`MON-2002`) |

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:69" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for Performance" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

PostgreSQL allows the application developer to specify the durability level required via replication. This can be specified for the system overall, though it can also be specified for specific users or connections, or even individual transactions.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:40" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

## External labels and remote read

If the querying Prometheus has `external_labels` that differ from or are absent on the remote server, queries may return no results because the matchers will not match. Ensure that any `external_labels` on the querying side are consistent with the labels present on the remote side.

Alerting rules allow you to define alert conditions based on Prometheus
expression language expressions and to send notifications about firing alerts
to an external service. Whenever the alert expression results in one or more
vector elements at a given point in time, the alert counts as active for these
elements' label sets.

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md" title="Remote Read API" section="Remote Read API > External labels and remote read" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:69" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for Performance" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

PostgreSQL allows the application developer to specify the durability level required via replication. This can be specified for the system overall, though it can also be specified for specific users or connections, or even individual transactions.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:40" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D06:2" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 2: Deploy it" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 2: Deploy it

Update the agent's secret to the new key and redeploy. New sessions pick up the new key; sessions already running finish on the old one.
</source>

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 4: Check for rate limiting

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D01:3" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Reading one agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

## Paging etiquette

When you page another team, say what you've already ruled out. "Registry slow, auth-service latency normal, registry-db CPU at 95%" gets a faster answer than "registry slow, please help."
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:15" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

From 2026-06-15 to 2026-06-22, `research_agent` answered questions with knowledge-base articles that had since been updated. Nothing failed and no alert fired; a user noticed that a report quoted a policy that had changed four days earlier.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

## When RegistryUnreachable fires

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

https://registry.internal.example/v2

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
